chapter_summary:
As your Unity project grows beyond a few simple objects, you'll quickly realize the need for a robust system to manage and reuse your game objects. Imagine building a city with hundreds of identical streetlights, or populating a forest with dozens of unique trees. Manually duplicating and configuring each instance would be incredibly time-consuming, prone to inconsistencies, and a nightmare to update. This is where **Prefabs** come in, forming the backbone of efficient asset management and scene construction in Unity.

At its core, a **Prefab** is a reusable Game Object asset stored in your Project window. Think of it as a blueprint or a template. When you create a Prefab, you're essentially saving a configured Game Object (complete with its components, child objects, and property settings) as a master asset. Any changes you make to this master Prefab asset are automatically applied to all its instances throughout your project, across all scenes. This powerful feature allows for rapid iteration, ensures consistency, and dramatically simplifies project maintenance.

The process of creating a Prefab from an imported 3D model is straightforward. First, you import your 3D model (e.g., the optimized barrel from previous chapters) into your Project window. Then, drag this model from the Project window into your Hierarchy. This creates a regular Game Object in your scene, which is an *instance* of the imported model. Now, you can configure this instance: add components like a Rigidbody, attach custom scripts, assign specific materials, set up colliders, or even add an LOD Group. Once your Game Object is configured exactly as you want it to be reusable, drag this configured Game Object from the Hierarchy *back into the Project window*. Unity will then prompt you to choose "Original Prefab." This action creates a new `.prefab` asset in your Project window, linking it to the Game Object you just dragged. The original imported model (e.g., `barrel.fbx`) remains the source of the mesh data, but the new Prefab (`barrel.prefab`) now represents the fully configured, reusable game object.

When you drag a Prefab from the Project window into a scene, you create a **Prefab instance**. These instances are visually distinct in the Hierarchy (usually with a blue icon) and are linked to their original Prefab asset. The beauty of instances is that while they inherit all properties from the master Prefab, you can also **override** specific properties on individual instances. For example, you might drag five instances of your `Barrel_Prefab` into a scene. You can then select one specific barrel instance and change its material color, or disable a script on another. In the Inspector, any property that has been overridden on an instance will appear in **bold** text, clearly indicating it deviates from the Prefab's default value. You have options to "Apply" these overrides back to the original Prefab (making the change global), "Revert" them (resetting the instance to the Prefab's default), or "Unpack Prefab" (breaking the link entirely, turning it into a regular Game Object, which should be done sparingly).

For even greater modularity, Unity introduces **Prefab Variants** and **Nested Prefabs**.
A **Prefab Variant** allows you to create a "child" Prefab that inherits properties from a "parent" Prefab. This is incredibly useful for creating variations of a base object without duplicating the entire asset. Imagine you have a `Tree_Base` Prefab. You could then create `Tree_Autumn_Variant` and `Tree_Winter_Variant` as Prefab Variants of `Tree_Base`. Any changes made to `Tree_Base` (e.g., adding a new component) would automatically propagate to both variants. However, each variant can also have its own specific overrides (e.g., `Tree_Autumn_Variant` has brown leaves, `Tree_Winter_Variant` has snow textures). This hierarchical approach to Prefabs is a powerful way to manage complex asset families. To create one, right-click an existing Prefab in the Project window and select "Create > Prefab Variant."

**Nested Prefabs** take modularity a step further by allowing a Prefab to contain other Prefabs as children. This means you can build complex structures from smaller, reusable components. For instance, you could have a `Car` Prefab that contains several instances of a `Wheel_Prefab`. The `Wheel_Prefab` itself might contain instances of a `Tire_Prefab` and a `Rim_Prefab`. This level of nesting allows artists to assemble intricate game objects from smaller, independently manageable parts, simplifying scene building and maintenance. If you update the `Tire_Prefab`, all `Wheel_Prefabs` (and thus all `Car` Prefabs) that use it will automatically update.

While primarily an artist's concern for efficient scene building, it's worth noting that programmers frequently use Prefabs for **runtime instantiation**. This means creating copies of Prefabs via script during gameplay, such as spawning enemies, projectiles, or power-ups. The `Instantiate(myPrefab, position, rotation);` function is a common way to achieve this, further highlighting the Prefab's central role in game development.

Common mistakes:
*   **Not Using Prefabs:** Leads to repetitive work, inconsistent assets, and difficult-to-manage projects.
*   **Breaking Prefab Connections:** Unpacking Prefabs unnecessarily means you lose the benefits of global updates. Only unpack if you truly need a unique, unlinked Game Object.
*   **Confusing Prefab Asset with Instance:** Remember, changes to an instance are local unless applied back to the Prefab asset.
*   **Over-nesting/Complex Prefabs:** While powerful, overly deep or complex nested Prefab structures can sometimes become difficult to navigate and manage. Find a balance that suits your project's complexity.

Safety note: Always ensure your Prefabs are saved correctly after making changes. If you modify a Prefab asset or apply overrides from an instance, make sure the changes are saved to disk. Unsaved changes to a Prefab instance that are not applied back to the master Prefab will be lost when you close and reopen the scene.

screens.title: Prefabs for Model Management & Instantiation
screens.subtitle: Blueprints for reusable Game Objects — efficient scene building, consistent updates, and runtime spawning.

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn what a Prefab is, why it becomes essential as a project grows, and how Prefabs connect imported model assets to configured, reusable game objects. A Prefab is a master asset that stores a configured Game Object — components, children, and property values — so you can place consistent instances across scenes. This saves time, reduces errors, and makes sweeping updates simple. We'll walk through creating a Prefab from an imported model, using instances, making and applying overrides, and the powerful patterns of Prefab Variants and Nested Prefabs. You will also see how programmers instantiate Prefabs at runtime to spawn objects during gameplay. By the end, you will understand not only the mechanics but the practical tradeoffs: when to keep a link to the master Prefab, when to unpack, and how to avoid over-nesting. For example, creating a single Barrel_Prefab lets you place hundreds of barrels and update them all by changing the master. Notice one common trap: unpacking too often removes the convenient global update. Keep that in mind as we explore the chapter.

screens.title: What is a Prefab?
screens.subtitle: A stored template for configured Game Objects and their settings

narration.text: A Prefab is a reusable Game Object asset that stores a configured object — components, child objects, property values, and references — as a single master. Think of it as a blueprint: the mesh data often comes from an imported model file like an FBX, but the Prefab stores the assembled, ready-to-use object you place in scenes. The practical benefit is consistency and speed. When you change the Prefab asset, every linked instance in every scene can update automatically. A common example: create a Barrel_Prefab with a Rigidbody, a collider, and an optimized material. Place many instances in a level; then change the material on the master to update all barrels. A frequent misconception is to treat the Prefab as merely a copy of the model. Instead, it holds configuration beyond mesh data. Another confusion is between the imported mesh asset and the Prefab asset: the mesh is the raw geometry, the Prefab is the configured object that references that mesh. Key takeaway: Prefabs let artists and developers make one authoritative setup and reuse it reliably. Ask yourself: which parts should be shared across all instances, and which should remain instance-specific?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A Prefab is a master asset that stores a configured Game Object so you can create consistent instances and update them globally.

Core Concept
What is a Prefab?
A stored template for configured Game Objects and their settings.
A Prefab stores assemblies: components, children, and property values. It references mesh assets but holds the configured object you reuse.
Key Takeaway

Prefabs centralize configuration so you can update one source and propagate changes to every instance.

Definition Card
Prefab = Configured Game Object Asset
Includes components, children, and default property values that instances inherit.
Concrete Example
Barrel_Prefab
Mesh from barrel.fbx, Rigidbody component, Box Collider, and LOD Group all saved in one Prefab asset.
Misconception
Prefab ≠ simple mesh copy
The Prefab contains configuration and references; the imported mesh remains a separate asset used by the Prefab.

screens.title: Create a Prefab from an Imported Model
screens.subtitle: Import, configure, then save a configured Game Object to the Project window

narration.text: The canonical workflow for creating a Prefab from an imported model has three steps: import the model, configure it in the scene, then save it as an Original Prefab. First, import your optimized mesh — for example, a barrel or a simple house model — into the Project window. Next, drag the imported model into the Hierarchy to create a scene Game Object instance. Configure that instance: add components such as Rigidbody, Box Collider, LOD Group, and assign materials. This in-scene configuration is what the Prefab will capture. Finally, drag the configured Game Object from the Hierarchy back into the Project window. Unity will create a. prefab asset and link the scene instance to it. Remember: the mesh source file remains the original import, while the Prefab asset stores the configured object. A common error is skipping configuration before saving, which results in a Prefab lacking required components. Another pitfall is making changes only to instances without applying them back. After creating the Prefab, test by placing several instances in a scene and verifying that shared changes update correctly. Create a Prefab from an Imported Model means import model → drag to hierarchy and configure → drag back to project to create an original prefab asset.. In practical terms, import, configure, then save a configured game object to the project window. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Prefab Instance vs Prefab Asset
screens.subtitle: How instances inherit, override, and relate to the master Prefab

narration.text: Understanding the difference between a Prefab asset and its instances is critical. A Prefab asset is the master template stored in the Project window. A Prefab instance is a copy placed into a scene that remains linked to the master. By default, instances inherit all properties from the asset. When you change a property on an instance, Unity marks that property as an override; the Inspector displays overridden values in bold to indicate deviation. Overrides are local until you apply them. Choosing Apply saves the override back to the master Prefab asset and propagates the change to all linked instances. Revert removes overrides on the instance and returns it to the Prefab's defaults. Unpacking severs the link entirely and turns the instance into an ordinary Game Object — use it only when you need a unique, unlinked object. An example: scale five instances differently — only their transforms change locally. If you meant to change the base scale, apply it on the Prefab asset. Misconception: changing one instance never automatically changes the asset unless you explicitly apply. Ask yourself: is this change for one special case, or should all instances inherit it?

keyIdea.title: Instance vs Asset
keyIdea.text: Instances inherit from a Prefab asset; overrides are local until explicitly applied, reverted, or unpacked.

content.html:
Comparison
Prefab Asset
Stored in the Project window as a .prefab file. Acts as the authoritative template for instances.
Prefab Instance
Placed in a scene, linked to the Prefab asset, can have local overrides shown in bold in the Inspector.
Apply Override
Save instance changes back to the Prefab asset to affect all instances.
Revert
Discard local changes and return to asset defaults.
Unpack Prefab
Break the link and make the object a stand-alone Game Object.
Concrete Example
Five Barrel Instances
Change color on one instance; the Inspector shows the material color in bold for that instance. Choose Apply to update the master or Revert to restore the original.
Misconception
"Editing one instance updates the asset"
Not true unless you Apply the override. Local edits remain instance-specific until applied.
Key Takeaway

Manage overrides intentionally: apply to share, revert to reset, unpack only when you need a unique object.

screens.title: Overrides: Detecting and Managing Differences
screens.subtitle: How Unity shows overrides and the decision to apply or revert them

narration.text: Overrides represent local edits on a Prefab instance. Unity flags overridden properties in bold in the Inspector so you can quickly see what deviates from the master Prefab. Typical overrides include material color, transform values, enabled/disabled components, or assigned scripts. When you see an override, decide whether this edit should be global or local. If the change should be shared, use Apply or Apply All in the Overrides dropdown to write the changes back to the Prefab asset. If the edit was accidental or specific to just this instance, use Revert or Revert All to reset it. Another option is Unpack Prefab, which removes the link and makes the instance a standalone Game Object; do this sparingly because you lose the ability to apply future global changes. A common mistake is to leave important fixes only on instances without applying them, then close the scene and lose the change. Conversely, applying accidental tweaks can propagate unwanted changes. Best practice: review overrides deliberately, use version control, and keep a habit of saving and testing after applying changes. In practical terms, how unity shows overrides and the decision to apply or revert them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Overrides Management
keyIdea.text: Overrides show local edits. Apply to save to the asset, revert to restore defaults, and unpack only when you need a permanent, unique object.

content.html:
Definition
Overrides
Properties edited on an instance that diverge from the Prefab asset. Shown in bold in the Inspector.
When to Apply
If the change should affect all instances, apply it to the Prefab asset.
When to Revert
If the change is local or accidental, revert to return to defaults.
When to Unpack
Only if you need an unlinked Game Object and are comfortable losing prefab linkage.
Concrete Example
Chimney Color Override
Change the chimney material color on a single House_Prefab instance. Inspector shows color in bold. Apply if every house should have that color; revert if it was only for one scene.
Mistake to Avoid
Applying accidental fixes across all instances can propagate undesired results. Revert when in doubt.

screens.title: Prefab Variants: Inheriting with Overrides
screens.subtitle: Create child Prefabs that inherit a base and add focused differences

narration.text: Prefab Variants create a family relationship: a Variant is a child Prefab that inherits the structure and properties of a parent Prefab but can contain its own overrides. This pattern is ideal when you need multiple related objects that share most behavior but differ in specific details. For example, create Tree_Base as the main Prefab, then make Tree_Autumn_Variant and Tree_Winter_Variant. If you add a component to Tree_Base later — say an interaction script — that change will propagate to variants, maintaining consistency. Variants also allow targeted differences: seasonal textures, different weapon attachments, or AI scripts. You create a Prefab Variant via the Project window using Create → Prefab Variant, or by right-clicking an existing Prefab. A misconception is that variants are copies that diverge completely; instead, they remain linked to the parent for shared updates. Use variants when you want inheritance with selective differences; avoid excessive variant chains that can complicate which layer controls a property. The takeaway: Prefab Variants let you design asset families efficiently while preserving a single point of maintenance for shared behavior. Prefab Variants: Inheriting with Overrides means a child prefab that inherits from a parent, allowing shared updates plus local overrides for variation.. In practical terms, create child prefabs that inherit a base and add focused differences. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Prefab Variant
keyIdea.text: A child Prefab that inherits from a parent, allowing shared updates plus local overrides for variation.

content.html:
Core Concept
Prefab Variants
Create variations of a base Prefab while retaining inheritance for shared changes.
Tree_Base → Tree_Autumn
Parent adds shared components; variant overrides leaf materials and color maps.
When to use
When many items share core configuration but need unique details.
Pitfall
Deep variant chains can obscure which Prefab controls a property. Keep variant depth manageable.
Concrete Example
Enemy_Base → Enemy_Ranged / Enemy_Melee
Share health and movement components on the base; add weapon models and AI scripts on each variant.
Check Your Understanding

Create a variant of House_Prefab and override only the roof material to make a RedRoof variant.

screens.title: Nested Prefabs: Compose from Reusable Parts
screens.subtitle: Assemble complex objects by nesting smaller Prefabs as children

narration.text: Nested Prefabs let you compose complex assets from smaller building blocks. Instead of a single monolithic Prefab, make smaller, focused Prefabs — for example, Tire_Prefab, Rim_Prefab, Wheel_Prefab, and Car_Prefab. The Wheel_Prefab contains Tire and Rim as nested Prefab instances; the Car_Prefab contains several Wheel_Prefabs. If you update the Tire_Prefab, all Wheel_Prefabs and all Cars using those wheels will receive the change. This pattern improves modularity and makes independent updates straightforward. A typical use case for artists: create a furniture set where drawers are nested Prefabs, enabling consistent behavior for every drawer across different furniture pieces. Be mindful of over-nesting: too many layers can make the Hierarchy hard to understand and slow editing. Also keep performance in mind when nesting many parts in runtime-instantiated objects. Best practice: design atomic Prefabs for parts you expect to reuse or update independently, and compose them into larger Prefabs for scenes. This reduces duplication and centralizes maintenance while keeping the assembly understandable. Nested Prefabs: Compose from Reusable Parts means build complex objects from smaller prefab parts so updates to a part propagate through assemblies that include it.. In practical terms, assemble complex objects by nesting smaller prefabs as children. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Nested Prefabs
keyIdea.text: Build complex objects from smaller Prefab parts so updates to a part propagate through assemblies that include it.

content.html:
Process Flow
Nested Prefabs
Compose assemblies by nesting reusable Prefab parts to allow updates at the part level to affect all assemblies that use it.
Atomic Parts
Create small Prefabs for parts you will reuse independently.
Compose
Nest parts into larger Prefabs for final assets.
Update
Change a part and see updates propagate across assemblies.
Watch Outs
Avoid overly deep nesting which complicates hierarchy navigation.
Example
Car_Prefab
Contains multiple Wheel_Prefabs; Wheel_Prefab contains Tire_Prefab and Rim_Prefab. Update Tire_Prefab to affect all wheels and cars that use it.
Why it matters

Nested Prefabs let teams reuse and maintain parts independently, keeping projects modular and efficient.

screens.title: Runtime Instantiation
screens.subtitle: Spawn Prefab instances from script during gameplay

narration.text: Programmers often instantiate Prefabs at runtime to spawn gameplay objects such as enemies, bullets, or power-ups. The basic runtime call creates a copy of the Prefab and places it into the scene at a specified position and rotation. A simple conceptual example is using Instantiate to spawn projectiles from a weapon. The artist's role is to ensure the Prefab contains the expected components: colliders, Rigidbody, visual materials, and any scripts the runtime will rely on. A common misconception is that runtime-instantiated objects do not connect back to the Prefab asset — they are instances created at runtime and are not linked in the Project window, but they still reflect the Prefab's initial configuration at the moment of instantiation. If you change the Prefab asset later, new instantiations use the updated configuration, but existing runtime copies do not auto-update. Best practice: keep Prefabs well-tested and consistent so runtime instantiation behaves predictably. The example code block shows the conceptual call; implementers will adapt to their scripting language and project patterns. Runtime Instantiation means instantiate a prefab at runtime to create gameplay objects; runtime copies use the prefab's current configuration at spawn time.. In practical terms, spawn prefab instances from script during gameplay. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Instantiate
keyIdea.text: Instantiate a Prefab at runtime to create gameplay objects; runtime copies use the Prefab's current configuration at spawn time.

content.html:
Application
Runtime Instantiation
Spawn Prefab instances from script to create gameplay objects on demand.
Developer Example
// Conceptual example of instantiation
GameObject spawned = Instantiate(myPrefab, spawnPosition, spawnRotation);
// spawned now has the components and default values from myPrefab at spawn time
Note: the example shows the idea; actual code will use the project's scripting conventions. Runtime clones are created in the scene and are not Project assets.
Artist Checklist
  • Ensure Prefab includes required scripts and components for runtime behavior.
  • Keep default values tested so spawned objects behave predictably.
  • Consider pooling for frequently spawned objects to improve performance.
Key Takeaway

Runtime instantiation uses the Prefab's current configuration at spawn; existing runtime copies do not auto-update when the asset changes.

screens.title: Prefab Organization & Naming
screens.subtitle: Keep Project and Hierarchy tidy for team collaboration and maintainability

narration.text: Organizing Prefabs and naming them consistently is a small effort that pays big dividends in team projects. Use clear, descriptive names that communicate intent and hierarchy, for example House_Prefab, House_RedRoof_Variant, Tire_Prefab. Group assets into folders: Props/Buildings/House_Prefab and Prefabs/Vehicles/Car_Prefab. When nesting, choose names that reflect composition: Wheel_Prefab contains Tire_Prefab and Rim_Prefab. This makes it easy for artists and programmers to find the right parts. Another recommendation is to keep Prefabs lean: include only what must be shared. Too many one-off changes end up as overrides, which can clutter the Inspector. Use variants for consistent family differences rather than creating many separate Prefab copies. Version control matters: commit Prefab changes frequently and test applied overrides before pushing. A common organizational mistake is scattering Prefabs across unrelated folders or naming them inconsistently, which creates confusion and slows iteration. Ask: will a teammate understand what this Prefab is for and where to find it? Prefab Organization & Naming means name and folder prefabs clearly, keep them lean, favor variants over duplicated assets, and commit changes to version control often.. In practical terms, keep project and hierarchy tidy for team collaboration and maintainability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Organization
keyIdea.text: Name and folder Prefabs clearly, keep them lean, favor variants over duplicated assets, and commit changes to version control often.

Best Practice
Prefab Organization & Naming
Use clear names and folder structures so teams can find and reuse assets easily.
Naming
Use descriptive names and suffixes such as _Prefab and _Variant.
Folder Structure
Group by type: Prefabs/Props, Prefabs/Vehicles, Prefabs/Characters.
Lean Prefabs
Keep shared configuration in the Prefab and avoid embedding scene-specific data.
Example Structure
Prefabs/Buildings/House_Prefab
House_Prefab and House_RedRoof_Variant live together for easy discovery.
Team Tip
Commit Prefab changes frequently
Test applied overrides before sharing changes to avoid breaking scenes for others.

screens.title: Hands-on: Create House_Prefab
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step lab to make an Original Prefab and exercise overrides

narration.text: Follow these hands-on steps to practice the full Prefab workflow. Start by importing a simple house model or use a cube placeholder. Drag it from the Project into the Hierarchy to create a scene Game Object. Add a child cube and position it as a chimney, add a Box Collider to the root, and assign a material. Now drag the configured Game Object back into the Project window and name it House_Prefab. Place several House_Prefab instances into a scene. Select one instance and change the chimney material color; observe the Inspector showing the override in bold. Use the Overrides dropdown to try Apply All and Revert All to see how changes propagate or reset. Next, right-click House_Prefab in the Project and choose Create → Prefab Variant to make House_RedRoof_Variant. Place the variant and change its roof material; confirm that the variant's change doesn't affect the original. This exercise reinforces the workflow and clarifies the difference between an instance, its overrides, and the asset. Practice until it feels routine. Scenario

Question

screens.title: Common Mistakes & How to Avoid Them
screens.subtitle: Practical advice to prevent lost changes, duplicated assets, and brittle hierarchies

narration.text: Several common mistakes recur when artists begin using Prefabs. First, not using Prefabs at all leads to duplicated objects across scenes and inconsistent updates. The fix is to create Prefabs early for any object you expect to reuse. Second, unnecessarily unpacking Prefab instances removes the link to the master and prevents future global changes. Only unpack when a unique, unlinked object is truly required. Third, confusing an instance with the Prefab asset causes unintended local edits to be lost; always decide whether to Apply or Revert an override before closing a scene. Fourth, over-nesting or creating excessive variant chains can make the hierarchy hard to understand and the source of bugs. Balance modularity with simplicity. Finally, failing to save or commit Prefab changes in version control risks losing work. Best practices: make Lean Prefabs, name assets clearly, keep atomic parts small, apply or revert overrides deliberately, and use variants for family differences. These habits protect project health and make collaboration predictable. Troubleshooting
Common Mistakes
  • Not using Prefabs → duplicated configurations.
  • Unpacking unnecessarily → lose master link and convenience.
  • Confusing instance edits with asset edits → lose changes when closing scene.
  • Over-nesting → complex hierarchies and harder maintenance.
  • Not saving Prefab changes in version control → lost or conflicting edits.
Remedies & Tips
Create early
Convert reusable objects into Prefabs as soon as they are stable.
Use variants
Prefer variants to duplicating similar Prefabs.
Version control
Commit Prefab changes regularly and test after applying overrides.

screens.title: Saving, Applying & Persistence
screens.subtitle: Ensure Prefab changes are saved to disk and propagated correctly

narration.text: A final operational concern is persistence: make sure Prefab changes are saved and consistent across sessions. When you apply overrides to a Prefab asset, Unity updates the. prefab file in the Project; however, unsaved scene changes or interrupted editor sessions can cause lost edits. Habitually save the scene and the Project after applying changes. Use version control to track Prefab changes so you can revert unwanted edits. When you apply an override, consider whether tests or a quick scene check are needed to confirm everything behaves correctly across levels. Also remember runtime-instantiated objects are created in-scene and will not reflect later asset changes; if you need persistent runtime modifications, write logic to update spawned objects or prefer applying changes to spawn points rather than runtime copies. Misconception: the Editor always writes every change to disk immediately; in reality, some operations require manual saves and source control commits to be safe. Make saving and committing part of your workflow to avoid lost work. Safety Note
Saving, Applying & Persistence
After applying overrides, save scenes and the Project, then commit Prefab changes to version control.
Quick Checklist
  • Apply overrides intentionally.
  • Save the scene and Project after changes.
  • Commit .prefab changes to version control.
  • Test across scenes after applying shared updates.
Runtime Note
Runtime Instances
Objects instantiated at runtime reflect the Prefab at spawn time and will not auto-update if the asset changes later.
Why it matters

Treat applying overrides and saving as a deliberate step; it avoids accidental data loss and keeps team collaboration stable.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from Prefabs and instantiation

narration.text: Here are the essential concepts to recall: First, a Prefab is a template asset that stores a configured Game Object, enabling consistent reuse. Second, Prefab instances inherit from the asset and show overrides in bold; apply or revert overrides deliberately to control propagation. Third, Prefab Variants allow you to create family members that inherit from a base while keeping their own differences. Fourth, Nested Prefabs let you compose complex objects from smaller parts so updates to a component propagate through assemblies. Fifth, runtime instantiation spawns Prefab copies during gameplay but does not retroactively update existing spawned objects when the asset changes. Finally, avoid common mistakes: do not unpack without reason, keep nesting manageable, and save and commit changes so you do not lose work. Use clear naming, lean Prefabs, and folders to support team collaboration. These ideas together make Prefabs a central tool for efficient, maintainable scene construction.

keyIdea.title: Core Takeaways
keyIdea.text: Prefabs centralize configuration, variants and nesting enable modularity, overrides control local edits, and persistence demands deliberate saving and version control.

Second, treat overrides as deliberate decisions: inspect bolded properties and choose Apply or Revert consciously. Third, prefer Prefab Variants and nesting over duplicating similar assets; they provide inheritance and modular updates. These quick rules help you avoid wasted time and maintain consistent scenes. Keep version control and regular saves part of your routine so Prefab changes persist across editor sessions. Use clear naming and folder structures so teammates can find assets quickly.
